headline: Oil fell hard in early November on hopes the US-Iran war is winding down, but the Strait of Hormuz is still not safe.
summary: Brent averaged $125 a barrel in October, its highest month since 2008, then dropped sharply in November as the US signaled no new strikes on Iran. Gold and silver slid as traders bet the Fed will raise rates in December. In food, sugar keeps climbing on El Niño while grain prices eased.

items.title: Oil drops about a fifth in November as war fears ease
items.text: Oil's October average of $125 a barrel was 93% above a year earlier. In November it fell about 20% after President Trump said new attacks on Iran were unlikely and the US kept its blockade instead, CNBC reported. The IEA's new report points to a growing oil surplus. The risk has not gone away: both sides reported ships hit near the Strait of Hormuz, and talks are stuck on Iran's nuclear material. A deal could push oil lower; renewed fighting could send it back up.

items.title: Gold and silver slide as a Fed rate rise looks likely
items.text: On 16 November gold was $3,876 an ounce and silver $47.42. Both are well off their monthly highs this year: gold averaged $5,020 in February, silver $92.10 in January. A hot US inflation report and tough talk from Fed officials have traders pricing an 85% chance of a December rate rise, and the dollar hit a near 19-month high, CNBC reported. Higher rates make metals that pay no interest less attractive.

items.title: World food prices dip again, but sugar keeps rising
items.text: The FAO Food Price Index fell for a third month in October, to 133.9, still 5.9% above a year earlier. Sugar went the other way: up 6.6% in the month and 28% in three months, its highest since December 2024. El Niño is the main worry. NOAA says it is still strengthening, with about a 60% chance it becomes one of the strongest on record this winter. Dry weather in Asia hits sugar first; palm oil usually feels it 6 to 12 months later.

items.title: USDA trims the US corn crop, raises world wheat stocks
items.text: The USDA's November report cut the US corn yield and lowered corn and soybean stocks, which tends to support those prices. It raised world wheat stocks, partly on a bigger world harvest. Wheat averaged $317 a tonne in October, down 8.6% from September but still 37% above a year earlier. Ample grain in storage is one reason food prices have stayed calmer than oil this year.
